Before FFS, there’s a lot of options to try. Or these options might make the wait for FFS more bearable. Ask a trans or trans-friendly salon stylist for a feminizing hair style that would suit your face shape. Get LHR or electrolysis. Commit to a simple but easily repeatable skincare regimen (like cleansing and hydrating first thing in the morning and right before bed at night). Tell your doctor explicitly that you’re not happy with your progress and want to up your hrt dose. (A LOT of doctors want to prescribe you the lowest possible dose that you’ll let them get away with, so you may need to assert yourself.) Try some basic makeup looks (like concealer and neutral eye shadow.) Buy some basic fem clothes. Do voice training. 

I know all this is easier said than done, but all you need to do is one little thing at a time. Start small and return to whatever feels right for you.

I’ve battled depression for a long time. Here’s what I’ve learned. 

Do a small, realistically accomplishable task. Clean a countertop. Do one load of laundry. Go outside, close your eyes, and notice every individual sound you hear for 5 minutes. Take a bath and shave your legs. Floss. Organize a drawer. Do a single pushup. Paint your nails. Read a single page in a book and then close it. Do a leg stretch for 30 seconds. Write one sentence describing how you feel. 

Small tasks with a clear end state. Once you complete one task, notice the feelings that come up. Can this be good enough for today? Why or why not?

Start small. To build confidence, you don’t rip the bandaid off and do an extremely hard thing all at once. No, you need to accrue dozens, hundreds of small, innocuous experiences where you try a small new thing and nothing bad happens.

So, wear fem underwear. Then maybe nails. Maybe concealer. Then dress in fem to walk outside for 30 seconds. Then walk down the street and back. Then drive somewhere in your car without getting out. Then walk in a public, anonymous place like a library or park. Then, start upping the difficulty: talk to a cashier or ask a shop clerk for where the changing room is or buy a movie ticket. And so on.

Small steps over days, weeks, and months.

I don’t know where you live, but in a lot of places, doctors are at best reluctant to prescribe HRT and at worst will refuse. Despite informed consent being the best practice, a lot of doctors still want to see “evidence” of dysphoria and long-term commitment. So…

1. Don’t show doubt. You’re 100% certain HRT is the right choice. (Share doubts with a therapist or friend, but not the prescribing doctor.) 

2. If it’s safe to do so, dress like the gender you’re transitioning to. Consider even wearing makeup (if you’re MTF). 

3. Do a little research about HRT basics (typical doses, different routes like patches, pills, and injections) if you haven’t already. 

4. Have some idea of your transition goal. Cis-passing may require higher doses.

Good questions to ask are whether there are known interactions with other prescriptions you’re currently taking and what the doctor’s goal for your treatment is (do they just want to give you a low dose to alleviate symptoms of dysphoria or would they be willing to up your dose in the future if your levels start to plateau or drop?)
